items.title: AI feedback does not motivate by itself: a motivational-meaning model for university physical education
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) can convert movement into scores, visual overlays, and corrective prompts, but technical precision does not determine how learners interpret that feedback. We develop a motivational-meaning model for university physical education (PE), integrating self-determination theory, feedback literacy, self-regulated learning, and motor-learning research. Its contribution is a context-specific account of how pedagogical framing, social visibility, and embodied verification organize the interpretation of an AI-feedback event. Informational and controlling meaning are distinguished from subsequent psychological-need experiences. Blocked translation denotes a temporary difficulty establishing a defensible basis for action, rather than a third motivational meaning. The model also proposes self-regulatory appropriation as the transfer of an externally supported feedback process into independent monitoring and adjustment; its distinctiveness from established self-regulation constructs remains an empirical question. Seven proposition groups specify separable predictions concerning framing, actionable information, contestability, evaluative exposure, discrepancy repair, skill transfer, and a secondary pathway to continued participation. The outcome structure distinguishes system engagement, acquisition performance, retention and transfer, affect and well-being, and voluntary physical activity. Continued participation is treated as a distal hypothesis requiring longitudinal evidence and attention to prior activity, health, habit, and opportunity. We outline independent measurement of event interpretation and need experience, tests that separate technical from perceived accuracy, and ethical, multilevel research designs. The model offers testable design principles rather than evidence that AI feedback improves learning or participation.

items.title: AI in smart cockpits: navigating compliance with the EU AI Act frameworks
items.abstract: The global smart cockpit market is undergoing explosive growth, with AI-enabled functionalities emerging as core components of modern vehicles. However, the integration of AI in smart cockpits has introduced complex compliance challenges under the EU AI Act and the General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR). This paper adopts a three-dimensional analytical framework (regulatory, technical, industrial practice) to systematically explore the compliance landscape, key dilemmas, and actionable solutions for smart cockpit AI systems. First, the paper clarifies the core obligations of high-risk and limited-risk AI systems under the EU regulatory framework. It also analyzes cross-regional regulatory conflicts among the EU, China, and the U.S., highlighting differences in data localization, consent mechanisms, and conformity assessment requirements. Second, the paper identifies risk-tier-specific compliance challenges, including data bias, transparency deficits, cross-border data transfer risks, as well as lifecycle management burdens. Additionally, it addresses emerging challenges brought by the integration of large language models (LLMs) in in-vehicle ecosystems, such as training data copyright verification and generative content controllability. Finally, the paper proposes an integrated compliance strategy. This strategy encompasses technical paths, full-lifecycle management, and cross-regional modular design to adapt to divergent regulatory requirements. The research provides a standardized compliance framework and practical tools for global automakers, helping balance technical innovation, user experience, and regulatory compliance to drive the sustainable development of the intelligent automotive industry.

items.title: AI Literacy among College Students and Its Influence on Academic Performance: A Study of Generative AI Tools
items.abstract: Abstract In today’s technology-driven world, Artificial Intelligence (AI) is becoming an important part of higher education. College students are increasingly using AI tools such as ChatGPT, Google Gemini, Microsoft Copilot, Claude, and Perplexity AI for their academic work. These tools help students prepare assignments and presentations, understand difficult topics, find ideas, improve their writing, and complete academic tasks in less time. However, simply knowing how to use AI is not enough. Students also need to understand whether the information provided by AI is correct, how to use it responsibly, and what problems may arise from depending too much on these tools. This study focuses on understanding the level of AI literacy among college students and its relationship with their academic performance. It will also study how familiar students are with generative AI tools, how often they use them, and for what academic purposes. The study will further examine the benefits students experience, the difficulties they face, and their understanding of issues such as academic honesty, originality, privacy, and responsible use of AI. The study will use a mixed-methods research design, combining both quantitative and qualitative methods. Quantitative information will be collected through a structured questionnaire using Google Forms. Interviews and open-ended questions will be used to understand students’ personal experiences, opinions, and attitudes towards AI in education. The study will include college students between 18 and 26 years of age from different academic backgrounds. The research will be limited to colleges in the Mumbai Metropolitan Region. The study is expected to provide a clear picture of how AI literacy is connected with students’ academic performance. The findings may also help colleges and teachers plan AI literacy programmes and create practical guidelines for the proper use of AI in education. Overall, the study aims to encourage students to use AI as a helpful learning tool while maintaining independent thinking, originality, and academic responsibility.

items.title: AI Policies Reduce but Do Not Eliminate the Moral Penalty of Using AI
items.abstract: Generative artificial intelligence (AI) now helps people write essays, reports, and even personal speeches, but people who use it can pay a social price through negative interpersonal judgement. We investigated whether people judge AI users as less moral, potential boundary conditions, and whether the policies that institutions set about AI use change this judgement. In six preregistered experiments with 2,183 participants from Belgium, the United States, and the United Kingdom, participants evaluated people who completed tasks either with or without AI assistance. AI users were consistently rated as less moral, as having invested less effort, as less deserving of their result, and as less attractive collaboration partners. The penalty was large, generalizable across context, and did not require a direct comparison with a non-user. Across studies, people who perceived a larger effort gap also judged the AI user more harshly. When the use of AI had been explicitly permitted, the moral penalty was attenuated by more than a third and when AI use had been prohibited, the penalty further increased. Clear AI policies may therefore reduce, but not remove, the reputational costs of using AI.

items.title: AI Safety as a Space between Fields
items.abstract: This chapter examines the novel task of making artificial intelligences safe through an analysis of 168 job postings from career platform https://www.w3.org/1999/xlink" xlink:href=" https://80000hours.org ">80000hours.org . Rather than viewing AI safety as a pre-paradigmatic field destined to solidify into clear professional boundaries, we analyse it as an interstitial network of expertise operating between academia, industry, government, and the non-profit sector. AI safety work, we find, takes place in a trading zone characterised by strategic ambiguity in organisational forms and domain expertise. This ambiguity stems from tensions built into the task itself: AI safety experts are expected to contribute to AI progress while attempting to control its risks, using dual-use methods that often advance both capabilities and oversight. These tensions shape hiring practices, with organisations seeking candidates who embody seemingly contradictory qualities – academic researchers and industry pragmatists, independent thinkers, and team players, highly specialised but effective communicators. We argue that such tensions are not temporary contentions to be resolved but rather constitute AI safety as a space between fields, attractive to multiple actors precisely because of its productive ambiguity.

items.title: Ai-Assisted Differentiated Instruction in Legal English: The Ailed Model
items.abstract: This article addresses one of the most important problems in the field of Legal English instruction: using artificial intelligence (AI) to organise effective, differentiated instruction for learners with diverse language skills. Legal English is a branch of English for Specific Purposes (ESP) that requires proficiency in legal terminology, legal genres, and legal discourse, as well as general language proficiency. Uniform instructional materials may be too challenging for some students and not challenging enough for others. The article proposes the AILED (AI-Assisted Legal English Differentiation) Model, which integrates AI-assisted differentiation of legal terminology, adaptation of instructional texts, and principles of differentiated instruction. The model has been developed after an in-depth review of literature on Legal English pedagogy, AI-assisted language learning, and differentiated instruction, as well as an analysis of placement-test data from 103 Master’s students enrolled in law and jurisprudence programmes at the International Scientific-Educational Center of the National Academy of Sciences of the Republic of Armenia. The placement data provide evidence of heterogeneous proficiency among law and jurisprudence students, supporting the need for differentiated Legal English instruction.

items.title: AI-Augmented Studio Pedagogy
items.abstract: The increasing integration of generative artificial intelligence (AI) into design practice has prompted product design education to reconsider the pedagogical foundations of studio-based learning. Although generative AI offers new opportunities for exploration, ideation, and design development, its unregulated use may undermine core designerly competencies, including reflective practice, material experimentation, and critical judgment. This article proposes an AI-augmented pedagogical framework that structures the integration of generative AI within the product design studio. Adopting a theoretically informed Research Through Design education approach, this study develops a pedagogical architecture articulated around four guiding principles, a five-phase studio model, and explicit regulatory mechanisms designed to support responsible AI use throughout the design process. The principal contribution of this article lies in the pedagogical operationalization of regulated co-intelligence. The proposed framework organizes interactions between students, teachers, peers, and generative AI systems in ways that preserve the foundations of designerly reasoning while fostering algorithmic reflexivity, critical AI literacy, and informed professional judgment. Designed as an adaptable pedagogical model, the framework provides a conceptual basis for future empirical research on the regulated integration of generative AI into studio-based design education.

items.title: AI-Based Fault Prediction for Small Solar PV Systems: An ESP32 Acquisition Unit and a Proposed Machine-Learning Framework
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) methods for photovoltaic (PV) fault diagnosis and prediction are usually developed on well-instrumented plants with reliable irradiance data and plentiful labelled examples, conditions that small, low-cost installations rarely meet. This paper presents a three-stage machine-learning framework for fault prediction in such installations, together with the ESP32-based acquisition unit that will supply its data. The unit is built and running. It measures PV voltage (GPIO34), current through an ACS712-20A sensor (GPIO35) and panel temperature through a DS18B20 sensor (GPIO4), computes power, and shows fixed-threshold status labels on a 16×2 I²C display. The AI framework is proposed and has not yet been implemented. Its first stage is an Isolation Forest trained only on normal-operation data, so that abnormal behaviour can be flagged before labelled fault data exist. Its second stage is a Random Forest classifier that assigns a fault class once staged-fault data have been collected. Its third stage predicts slowly developing faults: it fits trends to daily performance and thermal indices and estimates the number of days until each index crosses a fault threshold, giving an early warning before the fault becomes significant. Sudden faults such as open or short circuits cannot be predicted in this way and are only detected. All stages use features that combine raw measurements with physics-based residuals: the difference between measured power and the power expected from irradiance and panel temperature, and the difference between measured and expected panel temperature. A data-quality gate, a fault-class and labelling plan, a blocked train–test split and an evaluation protocol covering classification quality and prediction lead time are specified. No model has been trained, so no accuracy or prediction-error figures are reported; all pending results are marked.

items.title: AI-Driven Personalisation in Digital Payments: Examining Its Impact on Customer Trust
items.abstract: Abstract Digital India programme over a decade shown an upward performance by setting a benchmark. It is a flagship initiatives of the Government of India. It has digitally empowering the society and digital economy. Digital economy is an economic activities enhanced with the digital transformation using the digital computing tools. It provided various opportunities in the Banking and Fintech sectors. In current scenario Artificial Intelligence (AI) playing a very significant pivotal role by integrating the technology in all the sectors. It is enhancing the opportunities for the service provider and customer. Due to the rapid expansion of digital payment ecosystems, it has transformed the way how a consumers conduct their everyday financial transactions for purchasing their requirements either through online shopping i.e. e-commerce or visiting the store personal and using the digital banking or digital payment. In India, the digital payment especially using Unified Payments Interface (UPI) now has become a very important component of the digital financial ecosystem. Alongside this growth, the payment service providers are progressively integrating with the Artificial Intelligence (AI) technology to personalise their customer experiences. This is providing an enhance features through transaction recommendations to the customers with amazing discount features or offers in the payments using the digital payments. It further enables the customers in identifying their spending insights and intelligent alerts and adaptive customer support. This conceptual research proposes to examine the relationship between AI driven personalisation and customer trust in digital payment systems. The study propose to integrate from the perspectives of adopting the model Unified Theory of Acceptance and Use of Technology 2 (UTAUT2) with the trust theory. The proposed model considers AI personalisation, perceived usefulness, perceived relevance, transparency as among the key explanatory variables, with customer trust as the principal dependent construct. Behavioural intention and continuance intention are considered as potential outcomes of trust. The expected findings may provide very useful insight in the domain of digital banking, digital payment segment of the banks, fintech companies, and payment service providers to improve the trustworthy for the customer and responsible AI enabled payment ecosystems. Keywords: Artificial Intelligence, AI-driven personalisation, digital payments, UPI, customer trust.

items.title: AI-Driven Socratic Dialogues as Cognitive Scaffolds in Medical Scientific Writing
items.abstract: Medical students increasingly use large language models to generate manuscript text, bypassing the reasoning that scientific writing is meant to build. This monograph argues that the pedagogically defensible use of these tools is interrogative rather than generative. We map classical Socratic elements onto clinical writing tasks, compare the two architectures used to build Socratic writing tutors, describe how models are constrained to question rather than answer, and set out how to deploy such a coach in a medical curriculum. No study has yet tested this application directly; the supporting evidence is adjacent. A ready-to-use system prompt is supplied.

items.title: AI-Generated Deepfake Financial Scams: A Missing Liability Regime for Consumer Protection Frameworks
items.abstract: Abstract Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) outputs, such as deepfakes, can be useful for creating realistic simulations in education, news reporting, and the arts. However, the emergence of malicious deepfake scams has raised concerns about the quality and reliability of the information provided to social media users. This article argues that a liability regime for deepfakes is currently missing from consumer protection frameworks. Regulatory interventions do not explicitly target GenAI software developers and online social media platforms. However, the implementation of appropriate risk management safeguards is necessary to prevent unlawful deepfake activities. We contend that a shared liability regime for deepfakes among the multiple actors involved could offer adequate protection for victims of online financial fraud and would effectively target the deepfake supply chain. This shared liability regime would be complemented by the UK Financial Conduct Authority’s consumer duty rule, which acts as a preventive monitoring and enforcement mechanism to avoid foreseeable harm to consumers of AI applications.

items.title: AI-Powered Technologies in Foreign Language Education: Opportunities and Challenges
items.abstract: The integration of Artificial Intelligence (AI) into foreign language education has initiated an unprecedented paradigm shift within higher education institutions worldwide. This expansive research paper explores the multifaceted impact of AI-powered technologies in the English as a Foreign Language (EFL) classroom, critically evaluating the dual concepts of revolutionary pedagogical opportunities and systemic instructional challenges. Utilizing a comprehensive mixed-methods research design incorporating a quantitative survey of 115 university students and qualitative, structured interviews with language faculty members, this study analyzes tools ranging from automated speech recognition (ASR) systems to advanced generative artificial intelligence and large language models (LLMs). The opportunities identified and expanded upon include augmented student engagement, ubiquitous exposure to immersive, authentic language environments, personalized feedback loops, and a significant reduction in foreign language speaking anxiety through non-judgmental digital interfaces. Conversely, the critical challenges encompass algorithmic biases, digital divide inequities, the structural degradation of independent academic writing skills, cognitive dependency, and the profound loss of socio-pragmatic and cultural context in text generation. Ultimately, the paper argues that a balanced, hybrid pedagogical framework underpinned by proactive digital literacy is required to responsibly navigate these emerging dynamics, ensuring that artificial intelligence acts as a cognitive amplifier rather than a replacement for human-centered communicative interaction.

items.title: AI‐Driven Onboard Detection of Ocean Eddies by Haishao‐1 Spaceborne SAR
items.abstract: Onboard processing for remote sensing satellites has long been of interest in ocean monitoring because it can provide timely information on rapidly changing ocean environments. Recently, the integration of artificial intelligence (AI) into onboard processing has emerged as an active research topic. However, application scenarios and on-orbit demonstrations of AI-based onboard processing remain limited. In this study, we achieved the first on-orbit detection of ocean eddies using AI on the Haishao-1 (HS-1) spaceborne synthetic aperture radar (SAR) satellite, marking the first attempt to monitor an ocean dynamic process directly onboard. Specifically, an onboard application module was developed for HS-1, integrating image preprocessing and deep learning-based detection based on our previously developed Eddy Detection based on YOLO (EOLO) model. On-orbit experiments verified stable execution of the application module. Ground reproduction of the tasks using hardware identical to the onboard computing units yielded an average processing time of 3.4-6.1 s per image. Evaluation against expert annotations of 288 HS-1 scenes showed that EOLO, originally developed using Sentinel-1 imagery, achieved an F1 score of 78% after threshold adjustment. The application module has also been deployed on the Haishao-2 platform for Arctic sea ice extraction, further demonstrating its extensibility. This study presents the implementation and on-orbit validation of the onboard application module, providing a practical reference for future applications.

items.title: Algorithmic Management, Employee Voice, and Procedural Justice: A Governance Framework for Accountable AI-Assisted Organizations
items.abstract: Algorithmic systems increasingly allocate tasks, rank performance, flag anomalies, and recommend decisions that affect employment conditions. This critical integrative review examines how algorithmic management may reshape employee voice and perceptions of procedural justice in AI-assisted organizations. It distinguishes automated recommendations from fully automated decisions, information disclosure from effective contestability, and worker participation from symbolic consultation. Established research on algorithmic control, organizational justice, algorithmic transparency, and human-AI decision structures provides the conceptual basis. The article develops an accountability chain linking data provenance, decision rights, reviewability, employee explanation, correction pathways, and evaluation of organizational outcomes. It argues that the mere presence of a human reviewer does not demonstrate meaningful oversight; review authority, adequate information, and the ability to change an outcome are separate requirements. Potential benefits of automation include consistency and early detection of harmful errors, while risks include opaque sanctions, strategic data manipulation, and the displacement of responsibility. No primary interviews, experimental observations, or quantitative effect estimates are reported. The proposed empirical agenda combines process tracing, employee surveys, decision-log audits, scenario-based experiments, and organizational comparisons. The framework can be supported only if its specified safeguards improve measurable fairness, accuracy, employee trust, and organizational performance beyond existing governance practices. algorithmic management; employee voice; procedural justice; AI governance; human oversight; organizational accountability

items.title: AllPath: Layered Verification for a Deployed, Self-Revising LLM Trading Agent under Human-Gated and Autonomous Regimes
items.abstract: LLM trading agents are evaluated almost exclusively in backtests and autonomous benchmark harnesses. Deployment, where actions are irreversible, raises a different question: who verifies the agent's actions, and which failures can each verifier structurally catch? We report on AllPath, a personal LLM trading agent deployed against a live paper-brokerage account. The system watches positions through a deterministic rules engine, and each night it reviews its own day and proposes revisions to its own trading strategies. Verification is split across three layers. Code verifies what must not depend on judgment: deterministic gates enforce risk limits and block any strategy revision that fails an integrity check. The agent verifies itself within fixed bounds: its nightly review has an iteration cap and no tools that can act. A human verifies judgment, through approval screens that show the current state of each proposal. We also compared two verification policies for the agent's self-revisions on the live system: two and a half weeks with every self-revision human-gated, then five weeks with reflection revisions auto-applied behind the same code gates, while the operator's chat channel stayed human-gated throughout. Each layer caught a different kind of failure. The code gates rejected no proposal; their role was keeping revisions consistent. The human rejected two proposals that passed every code check, both over a disagreement about the market, and later removed 11 of the 19 rules the agent had added on its own, at a median lag of eight days. The most instructive production incidents, such as strategies silently left unmonitored, passed every gate; the operator found them by hand, and the fix each time was an interface change that makes the condition visible. We contribute the layered architecture, the two-regime account, and a production incident taxonomy, none observable in a backtest.

items.title: AN ARTIFICIAL INTELLIGENCE INTEGRATED PEDAGOGICAL PERSPECTIVE OF SECONDARY SCHOOL TEACHERS: A PHENOMENOLOGICAL STUDY
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is making a swift impact on the processes of teaching and learning by influencing lesson development, student assessment methods, and teachers’ perceptions of their profession. However, existing literature primarily focuses on the technical aspects of AI technologies rather than examining how secondary school teachers actually use these technologies when preparing lessons. The purpose of this study is to explore the experiences of secondary school teachers in using AI technologies in their teaching practices. Purposive sampling will be employed to select 15–20 teachers working with students in Grades 9–12 who have been using AI technologies for at least one semester. Data will be collected through semi-structured interviews and analyzed using content analysis. The findings are expected to provide a detailed understanding of teachers’ perceptions of AI integration into their professional practices, its influence on teaching and learning processes, the challenges and benefits they encounter, and the extent to which the use of AI tools shapes their professional identities.

items.title: An automated conversational speech-in-noise test using ChatGPT
items.abstract: Pure tone audiometry (PTA), the detection of tones in the quiet, is a widely used test to assess hearing ability, but it does not evaluate speech perception, even though difficulty hearing speech in background noise is the primary concern for most individuals with hearing loss. To solve this, speech-in-noise (SIN) tests are used as a more realistic representation of everyday communication. A common way of doing this test is by presenting stimuli (e.g., digits, sentences) to the person and asking them to repeat the stimuli. However, SIN tests have their issues: 1) Recording new stimuli requires special equipment and is an expensive and time-consuming process for researchers. 2) Most hearing clinics do not perform SIN tests, as they require spending more time on testing, which the audiologist cannot afford [1]. 3) Speech-in-noise (SIN) testing is a hearing assessment that aims to mirror natural conversation. However, the typical method involves repeating words, which does not reflect the flow of real-world conversations. To try and solve these issues, we are proposing a new SIN test that (i) uses text-to-speech (TTS) to generate stimuli (addressing problem 1), (ii) uses automatic speech recognition (ASR) and ChatGPT, a language model that generates human-like text responses based on user input, to transcribe and score participant’s responses instead of a clinician (address problem 2), and (iii) use ChatGPT and work towards creating a conversational and more natural test (address problem 3).

items.title: An empirical study on how social engineering and persuasion principles training affects senior citizens’ responses to SMiShing attacks
items.abstract: Purpose The purpose of this research study was set to address the problem of cyberattacks, such as phishing delivered via short message service (SMS) or SMiShing, targeted towards senior citizens. In 2023, they lost over $36m to such attacks. Phishing success increases when attackers use persuasion principles that bypass logical decision-making and rely on heuristics. Security education, training, and awareness (SETA) programs can reduce susceptibility, yet little research investigated SETA programs that incorporate these principles. Design/methodology/approach This research was conducted in three phases, beginning with Subject Matter Experts’ evaluation of SMiShing messages operationalizing these persuasion principles for use in this study’s instrument. The next phase was a pilot study. The third phase was the main data collection and analysis phase. This research employed a pretest-posttest design to evaluate the efficacy of its novel SETA program. The SETA program used Behavioral Skills Training methodology with 118 senior citizens from South Florida and Central Massachusetts. Findings The experimental results indicated a statistically significant mean difference between pretest and posttest group scores (F = 6.604, df = 5, p = 0.011) in identifying SMiShing messages that operationalize the principles of persuasion used in social engineering. Specifically, the pretest group’s mean score was 73.62, and the posttest group’s mean score was 79.28. The calculated effect size (η2 = 0.054) nears the threshold for a medium effect (η2 = 0.06). Practical implications Recognizing persuasion in SMiShing messages helped senior citizens better detect these cyberattacks. Practical implications include incorporating persuasion principles into the SETA framework to address evolving cyberattacks (e.g. deepfakes, vishing) that are being enhanced by generative artificial intelligence. Social implications As a group, senior citizens have lost millions to cyberattacks. SETA programs that incorporate principles of persuasion appear to help reduce the financial losses this group incurs from cyberattacks and may also improve senior citizens’ confidence and reduce fear when using communication technology. Originality/value This research’s original contribution is the integration of persuasion principles into cybersecurity training programs, helping senior citizens quickly recognize the malicious intent of SMiShing messages, which apply psychological pressures to achieve the attacker’s goals.

items.title: An LLM-Based Agent for Legal Compliance Assessment: Architecture, Memory, and Evaluation in a Canadian and Quebec Context
items.abstract: Checking whether a text complies with a body of law is slow when done by hand and fragile when done with keyword rules. This paper presents ComplianceAgent, the legal compliance sub-agent of COMPASS, a multi-agent framework that evaluates texts along four axes: digital sovereignty, carbon impact, compliance, and ethics. The agent relies on a large language model that scores a text on a fixed rubric, grounds its judgment in a reference legal corpus, and, when the score falls at or below a critical threshold, runs a corrective chain made of self-healing rewrites, a compliance label, an explainability report, and escalation to a human reviewer. We describe what the language model does at each step, how the memory of the agent is organized, and how the same implementation can be pointed at different reference corpora. We evaluate the agent in a Canadian and Quebec context, on a corpus of thirteen legal instruments that brings together federal and provincial texts, international treaties, and municipal documents of the City of Trois-Rivières. The evaluation relies on a hand-annotated gold standard of fifteen texts and combines classification metrics, a repeated-query stability test, retrieval precision, and a composite score. On this gold standard the agent separates every conforming text from every non-conforming one, its scores remain stable under repeated queries, and the index returns relevant passages.

items.title: Anatomy of Off-Policy Policy Gradient: Importance Sampling, KL Regularization, and Baselines
items.abstract: Reinforcement learning has become a central tool for large language model (LLM) post-training, where policy gradient methods are routinely deployed off-policy, even though vanilla policy gradient assumes on-policy sampling. We study when such off-policy deployment is justified, and what roles its core ingredients, including importance sampling, KL regularization, and baselines, play in handling the resulting distribution shift. We show that for a general class of off-policy policy gradient updates, consistency, in the sense that the optimal policy remains a stationary point, requires one of two structures at the optimal policy: trajectory-level importance weighting, which suffers from the well-known curse of horizon, or KL regularization with a baseline equal to the optimal soft value, instantiated by the grouped mean. Focusing on the KL route, we identify it with the group-relative policy gradient (GRPG) update, establish an equivalence to a trajectory-level Bellman residual minimization objective, and obtain a finite-sample regret bound under all-policy coverage. This also gives a theoretical account of a variant of the empirically successful GRPO objective. We further uncover a hidden role of baselines in the off-policy setting: a constant shift in the baseline implements pessimism, the standard remedy in offline RL for partial data coverage. We instantiate this via the asymmetric REINFORCE objective, and connect it to the game-theoretic offline RL framework, showing a regret bound with single-policy coverage. Together, these results offer a unified theoretical view of off-policy policy gradient in LLM post-training and connect it to classical ideas in offline RL.

Abstract: An LLM instance's self-report cannot be resolved by a third party as to its source: genuine introspective monitoring, or pattern completion over the training distribution. H3 (convergence) **not converged** — the measured self-first ratio 0.733 exceeds the ±0.10 tolerance window around the self-reported e₁₁ = 0.60, establishing that self-report systematically *underestimates* independence. Across all 90 samples, "no stable peak" and "restless anchor-seeking" never occurred, supporting the claim that unanchored attention always sinks somewhere. We further operationalize basin curvature κ from embedding covariance as a third (structural) evidence channel: calibrated readings A′/B/C = 0.664/0.690/0.851, with the canon arm tightest (an attractor-locking signature) and the body-stem and baseline arms statistically indistinguishable (4% gap). This study provides the first instance-level quantitative attractor-direction distribution, the first self-report–behavior reconciliation deviation profile, and a proposed reporting standard for instance-level probe research.

items.title: Answering While You Type: Optimizing Time-to-Answer with Streaming Generation
items.abstract: Work on efficient large-language-model inference has concentrated almost entirely on reducing the cost of decoding once a request is complete. The quantity a user experiences, however, is the interval between submitting a request and receiving a usable response, and that interval can be shortened without making decoding itself faster. While a request is being composed it is already partially specified, yet conventional deployments begin no computation until submission. We propose and study streaming generation, a decoding regime in which the model begins producing a response from an incomplete request and revises it as the remaining input arrives, so that only a small residue of the answer remains to be computed once the request is submitted. We evaluate the regime on autoregressive and diffusion language models, characterise the conditions under which it reduces user-visible latency, and analyse the mechanism responsible.

items.title: Aprendizagem de Inglês Mediada por IA: Estudo de Caso do Aplicativo FluentsLab
items.abstract: English language teaching faces persistent challenges related to learner motivation, linguistic immersion and the personalization of the learning process, particularly in contexts that rely on traditional grammar-translation methodologies. This article investigates how artificial intelligence based technologies contribute to English as a foreign language learning, using the FluentsLab application as the object of study. The general objective is to analyze the application's pedagogical resources, including contextualized immersion, educational games and an artificial intelligence based conversation robot, relating them to theoretical principles of second language acquisition, such as the comprehensible input hypothesis and sociocultural learning theory. The research adopts a qualitative, exploratory and descriptive approach, structured as a case study, combining a literature review on language teaching methodologies with documentary and functional analysis of the tools offered by the application. Results indicate that FluentsLab integrates gamification elements, simulated oral practice and content adaptation to the user's level, fostering greater engagement and consistent practice when compared to purely expository methods. Interaction with the conversation robot proves particularly relevant for oral fluency development, as it reduces barriers associated with the fear of making mistakes. The study concludes that the use of artificial intelligence in English teaching represents an effective complementary alternative to traditional approaches, expanding opportunities for authentic and personalized practice. The study reinforces the relevance of future research on the long-term impact of these tools on learners' language proficiency.

items.title: Are Self-Evolving Agents Continual Learners?
items.abstract: Large language model agents are often deployed in environments where new knowledge, tools, and workflows keep arriving. Such an agent is therefore expected to adapt continually, learning new tasks as they arrive without forgetting earlier ones. This resembles the continual learning problem, but at a pace that conventional gradient updates cannot sustain. Nonparametric self-evolving agents are a natural alternative: they adapt by rewriting their own harness, such as prompts, memory, and skills, from task feedback while the model weights stay frozen. We study whether such agents are effective continual learners across four drifting task streams that shift in topic, workflow, or domain (built from BIRD, BFCL, and ScienceWorld). Evaluating three representative methods spanning experience retrieval and self-modification (ReasoningBank, GEPA, and Meta-Harness), we find that although self-evolution improves aggregate performance on most streams, higher plasticity consistently comes at the cost of stability. Specifically, self-modifying methods apply global edits to a shared prompt or workspace, interfering with unseen tasks and overwriting earlier knowledge as the stream shifts. Conversely, similarity-based memory retrieval localizes updates across distant domains, but still retrieves foreign memories on unseen tasks and suffers from retrieval collision when similar queries require conflicting workflows. These findings show that current self-evolving agents remain incomplete continual learners.

items.title: Are the Eyes a Mirror of Autism? Explainable AI-Based Biomarker Discovery for Diagnosis
items.abstract: Autism spectrum disorder (ASD) presents significant difficulties in diagnosis due to its nature and diversity of symptoms. Traditional diagnostic methods rely on comprehensive clinical evaluations and complex diagnostic processes. Recent advances in machine learning (ML) and explainable artificial intelligence (XAI) offer promising models that help improve diagnostic accuracy and efficiency in ASD. XAI methods provide explainability by determining feature importance and indicating the extent to which features impact the outcome. In this study, we use children’s eye-tracking data and propose using this capability of XAI as a feature selection (FS) method in ASD diagnosis. Specifically, we aim to compare the performance of XAI-based and traditional FS methods individually and explore the benefits of combining these approaches. The goal is to enhance the diagnostic accuracy of ML models while simultaneously identifying significant features—a process referred to as biomarker discovery—through the proposed system. This system enables the identification of critical features that differentiate children with ASD from their typically developing (TD) peers, offering valuable insights to clinicians for improved diagnostic practices. The results demonstrate that the XAI-based FS method improves model performance compared to traditional feature selection techniques, with the highest AUC score of 0.78 achieved by combining feature sets from both methods. Furthermore, the XAI approach successfully identified four candidate biomarkers critical to ASD diagnosis, which were not selected by traditional methods. These findings underscore the potential of XAI techniques not only to boost model accuracy but also to uncover new diagnostic insights. By combining the XAI-based FS method with traditional approaches, this research contributes to advancing diagnostic practices in ASD, identifying new biomarkers, and enhancing clinical decision-making in pediatric neurodevelopmental disorders.

items.title: ARTIFICIAL INTELLIGENCE (AI) AND CHANGE MANAGEMENT IMPLEMENTATION IN THE NIGERIAN OIL AND GAS BUSINESS ENVIRONMENT
items.abstract: Abstract This study examines the relationship between artificial intelligence (AI) and change management implementation in the Nigerian oil and gas business environment. Focusing on three dimensions of AI (predictive analytics, robotic process automation, and AI-enhanced decision support systems), the study investigates how these technologies influence the effectiveness of change management initiatives within the Nigerian upstrea petroleum sector. Anchored in the Technology Acceptance Model (Davis, 1989) and the Dynamic Capabilities Theory (Teece et al., 1997), the research adopts a cross-sectional survey design, drawing data from 98 valid respondents comprising managerial and technical employees across 15 oil and gas firms in Rivers State, Nigeria. Using Pearson Product-Moment Correlation Coefficient (PPMC) and Multiple Regression Analysis, findings reveal strong, positive, and statistically significant relationships between all three AI dimensions and change management implementation. AI-enhanced decision support systems and predictive analytics emerged as the strongest predictors of change management outcomes. The regression model accounts for 64.3% of the variance in change management implementation, underscoring the substantial explanatory power of AI technologies in organizational transformation. The study recommends that Nigerian oil and gas firms strategically invest in AI infrastructure, build AI-competent workforces, and align AI deployment with their change management frameworks to enhance transition effectiveness and sustain competitive advantage in a rapidly evolving industry. Keywords: Artificial Intelligence, Change Management Implementation, Decision Support Systems, Nigerian Oil and Gas, Predictive Analytics, Robotic Process Automation.

items.title: Artificial intelligence and machine learning for meta data management in libraries: a computational analysis
items.abstract: Purpose This study explores the growth, trends and patterns of scholarly research by using bibliometric and computational methods. This study aims to identify prolific authors, influential journals, collaborative networks and emerging themes. This paper offers insights into how Artificial Intelligence (AI) and Machine Learning (ML) are transforming metadata practices to enhance information organisation, retrieval and interoperability. Design/methodology/approach A structured three-phase methodology was adopted. At first, appropriate keywords were identified, and the required data was extracted from the Scopus database (2010–2024) using a Boolean search string. Of 3,624 records, 3,424 articles were found relevant after removal of irrelevant articles manually. Software such as Biblioshiny and VOSviewer were used to analyse the trends in publication, citation patterns, co-occurrence of keywords and the collaborative patterns. Social Network Analysis was applied to map the co-authorship patterns, collaboration at institutional and country levels. Findings The results of this study indicate steady growth in AI and ML research in library metadata, though citation impact has declined since 2018. Kanwal Ameen is the most productive author, and the USA is the most productive country. Dominance by a few journals and authors aligns with Bradford’s and Lotka’s Laws. The collaboration pattern remains limited among authors and countries. Thematic evolution shows a shift from traditional metadata access to intelligent technologies like AI, ML and IoT. Regional collaborations are stronger than author-level links, and recent trends align with broader digital transformation Originality/value To the best of the authors’ knowledge, this is the first known study to comprehensively examine AI and ML applications in library metadata management through computational bibliometric analysis.

items.title: Artificial Intelligence and Machine Learning in Solubility Enhancement of Poorly Water-Soluble Drugs: From Solubility Prediction to Formulation Optimization
items.abstract: Poor aqueous solubility limits the development of many orally administered drug candidates, particularly those in Biopharmaceutics Classification System (BCS) class II and, in some cases, class IV. Conventional solubility-enhancement approaches, including particle-size reduction, solid dispersions, amorphous systems, lipid-based formulations, cyclodextrin complexation, nanocrystals, salt formation and pharmaceutical cocrystals, are effective but often require extensive, formulation-specific experimentation. Growing pharmaceutical datasets and advances in artificial intelligence (AI) and machine learning (ML) now offer predictive, data-driven support. Models have been reported for predicting aqueous and formulation-phase solubility, screening drug-excipient combinations, estimating drug-polymer interaction, optimizing compositions and predicting dissolution or supersaturation behaviour. Bayesian optimization, active learning and surrogate modelling are being explored to reduce the number of formulation experiments, and integration with physiologically based pharmacokinetic (PBPK) modelling, Quality by Design (QbD) and automated experimentation may further support rational development. However, small and heterogeneous datasets, experimental variability, limited interpretability and external validation, data leakage and uncertain regulatory acceptance remain significant barriers. This review discusses AI and ML in the solubility enhancement of poorly water-soluble drugs, progressing from molecular solubility prediction to drug-excipient selection, advanced formulation design and formulation optimization. Particular emphasis is placed on experimentally validated applications and on the distinction between computational prediction and demonstrated pharmaceutical performance. Current challenges, research gaps and opportunities for reliable, explainable and experimentally integrated AI-driven formulation platforms are outlined.

items.title: Artificial Intelligence and Social Inequality: A Review of Algorithmic Bias, Digital Exclusion, and Governance Responses
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly integrated into employment, education, healthcare, financial services, public administration, and social welfare systems, creating opportunities to improve efficiency, accessibility, and decision-making. However, the growing reliance on AI also raises concerns about social inequality, particularly when algorithmic systems reproduce existing patterns of discrimination, exclude marginalized populations, or concentrate technological benefits among already advantaged groups. This review examines the relationship between AI and social inequality, focusing on algorithmic bias, digital exclusion, and emerging governance responses. It synthesizes conceptual and empirical literature on discriminatory data practices, unequal access to digital infrastructure, disparities in AI literacy, and the socioeconomic consequences of automated decision-making. The review also examines how inequalities associated with gender, race, socioeconomic status, disability, geography, and language can influence the design, deployment, and outcomes of AI systems. The literature indicates that algorithmic discrimination may arise from unrepresentative datasets, historical inequalities embedded in training data, inappropriate performance measures, and insufficient institutional accountability. Digital exclusion further limits the capacity of disadvantaged populations to benefit from AI-enabled services, particularly in contexts characterized by inadequate connectivity, limited digital skills, affordability constraints, and linguistic barriers. Although regulatory frameworks, algorithmic audits, inclusive design, and human oversight offer important safeguards, their effectiveness depends on implementation, transparency, and meaningful participation by affected communities. The review argues that addressing AI-related social inequality requires an integrated approach combining technical fairness, digital inclusion, institutional accountability, and rights-based governance. It concludes that AI should be evaluated not only in terms of technological performance but also according to its contribution to social justice, equitable access, and inclusive development.

items.title: Artificial Intelligence Applications in Anesthesiology: A Comprehensive Narrative Review
items.abstract: Background: The integration of artificial intelligence (AI) and machine learning (ML) technologies in anesthesiology has emerged as a transformative force in perioperative medicine. This narrative review synthesizes current evidence on AI applications across the perioperative continuum. The objective is to provide a comprehensive overview of AI applications in anesthesiology, examining current implementations, clinical outcomes, and future directions across preoperative assessment, intraoperative monitoring, drug delivery, postoperative care, and clinical documentation. Methods: A systematic literature search was performed across several databases for peer-reviewed publications on AI applications in anesthesiology from 2015 to June, 2025. If the papers were peer reviewed and come from quality journals. Sixty-six papers from reputable peer-reviewed medical journals of high quality were selected for analysis. Results: The use of AI-based applications for anesthesiology can be summarized into 5 specific domains: predictive modeling to predict surgical risk assessment, real-time monitoring systems that measure anesthesia depth, automated drug delivery systems (and devices), postoperative complication prediction after surgery, and natural language processing (NLP) to assess clinical documentation. Recent advances show better patient outcomes, clinical decision-making and operational efficiency. Conclusion: AI technology holds substantial potential to enhance anesthesiology practice along the entire perioperative continuum. Although some challenges need to be addressed in respect of clinical integration and validation, we believe that there is sufficient evidence to justify undertaking further development work with a view towards implementation of AI-assisted anesthesia care.

items.title: Artificial intelligence applications in long-term care facilities: a scoping review across planning, design, operation, and assessment
items.abstract: Introduction Improving the quality of long-term care facilities (LTCFs) is critical to safeguarding the health, safety, dignity, and quality of life of older adults amid global population aging. However, traditional design methods for LTCFs rely heavily on static codes and empirical judgment, limiting their ability to respond to dynamic care needs and balance multiple objectives across lifecycle stages. To address these limitations, artificial intelligence (AI) offers a promising solution through dynamic optimization and intelligent decision-making. Methods A scoping review was conducted to systematically map the applications of AI in LTCFs across four lifecycle stages: planning and site selection, architectural design, operation and management, and assessment and retrofit. Searches were performed in Web of Science, Scopus, Google Scholar, SAGE Journals, and CNKI for literature published between January 2010 and December 2025, resulting in the inclusion of 38 eligible publications. The review was guided by the methodological framework proposed by Arksey and O’Malley and reported in accordance with PRISMA-ScR. Results Four main application pathways were identified, including prediction and evaluation, generation and evolution, sensing and recognition, and simulation and modeling. Specifically, AI was applied to site-selection evaluation and demand forecasting during planning; spatial layout generation and intelligent equipment integration during design; safety monitoring, behavior recognition, and environmental control during operation; and comfort and safety assessment and retrofit optimization during assessment. Research was concentrated in operation and management, whereas evidence on assessment and retrofit remained limited. Discussion Overall, AI shows potential to shift LTCFs from static, fragmented, and experience-based practices toward more data-informed, adaptive, and person-centered care environments. However, implementation remains constrained by data quality and standardization, facility heterogeneity, system integration, equitable access, privacy, and ethical concerns. This review provides planners, architects, engineers, care providers, facility managers, and public health decision-makers with a technology roadmap and identifies priorities for using AI-enabled built environments to support high-quality older adult care and sustainable long-term care systems.

items.title: Artificial Intelligence As A Learning Partner: Rethinking The Roles Of Teachers, Learners, And Knowledge Construction In Contemporary Education
items.abstract: The rapid development of generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) has transformed how teachers and students access, process, and construct knowledge in contemporary education. The increasing capacity of AI systems to provide information, generate ideas, support dialogue, and offer feedback raises fundamental questions about the changing roles of teachers and students and the position of AI within the learning process. This study aims to analyze the conceptualization of AI as a learning partner and examine its implications for teacher roles, student agency, and knowledge construction. This qualitative study employs a Systematic Literature Review (SLR) with thematic-conceptual synthesis. Relevant literature was identified through Google Scholar, supported by Consensus as a supplementary literature discovery and verification tool. The reviewed literature was analyzed through thematic coding, categorization, comparison, and conceptual synthesis. The findings indicate two major patterns. First, the involvement of AI shifts the role of teachers from primary transmitters of information toward pedagogical guides, knowledge curators, dialogue facilitators, and validators of information and educational values, while students are increasingly positioned as active agents who question, evaluate, interpret, and reflect on AI-generated information. Second, knowledge construction becomes more relational, involving the interaction of teachers, students, and AI through processes of generation, verification, interpretation, negotiation, and reflection. AI therefore functions as a cognitive learning partner rather than a final epistemic authority. The study contributes a conceptual framework that integrates the teacher as a pedagogical agent, the student as an epistemic agent, and AI as a cognitive partner while maintaining human agency at the center of education.

items.title: ARTIFICIAL INTELLIGENCE AS A TOOL FOR PERSONALIZED ENGLISH LANGUAGE LEARNING
items.abstract: Traditional language education classrooms often struggle to accommodate the diverse learning paces, styles, and proficiency levels of individual students. This research paper explores the role of Artificial Intelligence (AI) as a transformative mechanism for personalized English language learning in higher education. By analyzing various AI-driven educational applications, intelligent tutoring systems (ITS), and adaptive learning platforms, this study examines how technology customizes linguistic input, provides real-time corrective feedback, and establishes individualized learning pathways. Utilizing a mixed-methods approach, the study surveys 120 undergraduate students to measure their engagement and perceived language acquisition progress when utilizing AI tools. The findings demonstrate that AI significantly enhances learner autonomy and vocabulary retention by adapting to the student's unique Zone of Proximal Development (ZPD). However, the paper also addresses critical limitations, including the lack of socio-cultural nuance in AI communication and the risk of reduced authentic interpersonal interaction. The study concludes with practical recommendations for integrating adaptive AI platforms into university EFL curricula to foster an optimized, student-centered learning environment.

items.title: Artificial intelligence at work: a socio-psychological model of employee adoption and innovation
items.abstract: Purpose This research aims to identify the key organisational, cognitive, and psychological predictors of perceived usefulness of artificial intelligence (AI) and to evaluate their influence on the AI adoption intention and innovative behavior of employees in the Jordanian setting. Design/methodology/approach A strict quantitative research design was adopted in the current study in which a structured online questionnaire was conducted among employees working in various industries in Jordan, mainly IT, retail, and banking. Quantitative data comprising 388 valid responses were then analyzed using partial least squares structural equation modeling to assess both the direct effects as well as moderating relationships between the constructs of interest. Findings The results show that organizational culture (β = 0.216), technology usage habits (β = 0.278), and AI self-image (β = 0.195) positively influence AI perceived usefulness, while AI literacy significantly reduces AI anxiety (β = −0.482). AI perceived usefulness strongly predicts employee innovative behavior (β = 0.608) and AI adoption intention (β = 0.657). Job insecurity weakens the relationship between perceived usefulness and adoption intention (β = −0.234), but its moderating effect on innovative behavior is insignificant. AI anxiety also weakens the effects of perceived usefulness on adoption intention (β = −0.208) and innovative behavior (β = −0.180). Originality/value A socio-psychological approach is used in this investigation, highlighting the significance of identity congruence and the importance of affective processes in the adoption of AI. It anticipates psychological and emotional engagement of employees in AI, breaking the false belief that acceptance is dictated by technical or rational factors only.

items.title: Artificial intelligence detects the dismantling of nutrient co-occurrence architecture by ultra-processing: explainable machine learning and network analysis of 22,481 usda-classified foods
items.abstract: Abstract Ultra-processed foods have been linked to 32 adverse health outcomes in an umbrella review of epidemiological meta-analyses spanning evidence published between 2009 and 2023, yet the nutritional mechanism underlying these associations remains poorly characterised at scale. We constructed UPFNet, an artificial-intelligence framework that couples nutrient co-occurrence network analysis with explainable machine learning across 22,481 foods from two USDA composition databases spanning 788,582 measurements across 33 nutrients, with NOVA group assignment via a validated 67-term keyword algorithm. Vitamin C, water, vitamin B12 and protein were depleted by 85.7%, 81.8%, 81.2% and 63.4%, respectively, in NOVA 4 relative to NOVA 1 (all p < 10−9; 27 of 33 nutrients survived Bonferroni correction). The whole-food co-occurrence network held 249 edges, whereas the ultra-processed network retained only 162, a 34.9% collapse (KS = 0.195; p = 3.37 × 10−9). The dominant hub shifted from fibre (betweenness centrality 0.790) to water (0.940). Gradient boosting classification achieved an AUROC of 0.9848 (95% CI 0.9793–0.9903), an accuracy of 94.2%, and a fold coefficient of variation of 0.29%, with mean-decrease-in-impurity attribution identifying energy, water, carbohydrate, sodium and protein as the five dominant discriminative features. Industrial processing fundamentally dismantles the architecture of nutrient co-occurrence, not merely individual nutrient content.

items.title: Artificial intelligence for ophthalmic vessel segmentation: from multimodal imaging to clinical translation
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI)-based vessel segmentation converts color fundus photographs, scanning laser ophthalmoscopy (SLO), optical coherence tomography angiography (OCTA), structural OCT, and anterior-segment images into quantitative vascular biomarkers. Strong performance within individual datasets has not consistently yielded reliable clinical measurements because errors can arise during acquisition, anatomical preprocessing, vessel extraction, biomarker calculation, and deployment. This structured narrative review compares segmentation tasks involving retinal vascular trees, OCTA capillary plexuses, the structural choroid and choriocapillaris, macular neovascularization, corneal neovascularization, and conjunctival microvasculature. We assess modern architectures in relation to vessel geometry, severe foreground-background imbalance, scale variation, crossings, and susceptibility to artifacts. The methods considered include multiscale feature pyramids, deformable and directional operators, Transformers, state-space models, diffusion approaches, and foundation models. We organize the synthesis around five evaluation levels: pixel overlap, centerline recovery, vascular topology, biomarker agreement, and clinical actionability. Public fundus and OCTA datasets are catalogued with their acquisition and annotation characteristics, and gaps in public anterior-segment vessel benchmarks are discussed. Because devices, data splits, labels, and post-processing differ substantially, reported metrics are summarized without ranking studies against one another. The review distinguishes structural OCT choroidal vascularity index from OCTA choriocapillaris flow-deficit mapping, as well as true vessel segmentation from global hyperemia grading. Clinical translation will require ocular-magnification correction, quality control of retinal layers and projection artifacts, external testing across devices and populations, out-of-distribution rejection, DICOM/PACS interoperability, prospective impact studies, and regulation as software as a medical device. We conclude that clinical utility depends on an auditable pipeline that measures structural error, biomarker uncertainty, and failure states throughout the workflow.

items.title: Artificial Intelligence Impact on Productivity and Economic Growth
items.abstract: The increasing diffusion of AI has generated considerable interest among economists and management scholars, because technological change is a fundamental source of long-term productivity and economic growth. In conventional growth theory, technological progress enables economies to produce more output from a given quantity of labour and capital. AI may influence this process by increasing the efficiency of existing production activities, augmenting workers’ capabilities, accelerating research and development, and improving the allocation of organisational resources. Unlike many earlier digital technologies, AI can perform tasks involving prediction, classification, information processing, content generation and decision support. Consequently, its potential economic effects extend beyond the automation of routine activities to include innovation, organisational transformation, human– machine collaboration and the creation of new products and business models. AI should not be considered an automatic source of economic growth. The productivity consequences of a new technology depend on complementary investments, organisational capabilities, institutional conditions, and the ability of workers and managers to incorporate the technology into production processes. AI can increase aggregate productivity and economic output, but the benefits may not be distributed equally. There are several risks, such as displacement of workers performing automatable tasks, wage polarisation, concentration of technological capabilities, advantages for large firms and divergence between technologically advanced and less-prepared economies.

items.title: Artificial Intelligence in Drug Discovery and Pharmacology: Applications, Advances, Challenges, and Future Perspectives
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is becoming a powerful helper in pharmaceutical research, especially in finding and developing new drugs. Traditional drug development is slow, expensive, and complicated, involving many steps from identifying disease targets to final regulatory approval. AI tools—such as machine learning, deep learning, and natural language processing—can quickly analyze huge amounts of data, opening new ways to improve this process. This review explains how AI is used in key areas like finding drug targets, screening molecules, designing new drugs, predicting safety and side effects, understanding how drugs behave in the body, repurposing old drugs, and supporting clinical trials and personalized treatment. AI helps researchers choose better drug candidates, predict risks, and make treatment plans more tailored to individual patients. The article also highlights popular AI platforms that combine chemical, biological, and clinical data. However, challenges remain: data can be incomplete or biased, AI models are sometimes hard to interpret, and predictions don’t always match real-world results. For these reasons, AI should be seen as a support tool—not a replacement—for lab work, clinical trials, and expert judgment. Looking ahead, the field is moving toward more advanced AI that can handle multiple data types, generate new molecules, model protein structures, and connect lab and clinical workflows more seamlessly.

items.title: Artificial Intelligence in Finance and Accounting: A Critical Review of Applications, Transformative Impact, Challenges and Future Research Directions
items.abstract: Abstract Artificial Intelligence (AI) is progressively reshaping the conceptual and operational foundations of finance and accounting. What began primarily as the automation of routine and rule-based processes has evolved into the application of machine learning, deep learning, natural language processing, predictive analytics and intelligent automation to increasingly complex financial and accounting decisions. Against this background, the present paper critically reviews the literature on the impact of AI on finance and accounting, with particular attention to financial forecasting, bankruptcy prediction, financial statement analysis, auditing, fraud detection, credit-risk assessment, investment analysis, organizational performance and professional transformation. The review demonstrates that AI has considerable potential to enhance computational efficiency, predictive capability, anomaly detection and decision support. However, the literature does not establish technological superiority as an automatic consequence of AI adoption. Rather, the effectiveness of AI is contingent upon data quality, model selection, organizational readiness, employee competencies, governance arrangements and the ability of professionals to interpret algorithmic outputs. An important theme emerging from the literature is the transition of accounting and finance from predominantly retrospective and transaction-oriented functions toward more predictive, analytical and strategically embedded roles. At the same time, increased reliance on algorithmic decision-making introduces concerns relating to explainability, bias, data privacy, cybersecurity, professional accountability and regulatory oversight. The review therefore argues that the long-term significance of AI lies less in the replacement of finance and accounting professionals than in the reconfiguration of professional work through human-AI complementarity. The paper concludes by identifying gaps concerning implementation, longitudinal organizational outcomes, explainable AI, professional competencies and emerging-economy contexts, thereby providing directions for future research. Keywords: Artificial Intelligence, Finance, Accounting, Machine Learning, Auditing, Financial Forecasting, Fraud Detection, Risk Management, Professional Transformation, Human-AI Collaboration

items.title: Artificial intelligence in food safety: a bibliometric and empirical synthesis of emerging technologies and research frontiers
items.abstract: Purpose This study aimed to identify recent research trends in the integration of artificial intelligence (AI) with food safety and security through a comprehensive bibliometric analysis. Design/methodology/approach A total of 2,782 documents published between 2021 and 2025 were retrieved from the Web of Science Core Collection. The dataset was refined by removing duplicates, filtering document types and excluding irrelevant records. VOSviewer was then used to conduct co-authorship, keyword co-occurrence, citation, co-citation and bibliographic coupling analyses. Findings Machine learning and deep learning emerged as core technologies associated with food security, contamination detection and quality prediction. Keyword clustering demonstrated interdisciplinary connections with agriculture, climate change and public health. Citation and co-citation analyses identified three major intellectual foundations: traditional machine learning, computer vision-based deep learning and time-series modeling. China, India and the United States were the most influential contributors in terms of research output and technological development. Bibliographic coupling and source co-citation analyses further indicated increasing convergence between food science and computational science. Originality/value This study provides a comprehensive overview of the intellectual structure, collaborative networks and thematic evolution of AI-driven food safety research. Unlike previous studies focusing on specific technologies or applications, it maps global research patterns and interdisciplinary linkages. The findings provide strategic insights for researchers, policymakers and industry stakeholders. Future studies should prioritize explainable AI integration into regulatory frameworks and the development of larger, more diverse datasets to improve model generalizability across food systems.

items.title: Artificial Intelligence in Human Resource Management: A Systematic Literature Review, Integrative Framework, and Future Research Agenda
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is reshaping Human Resource Management (HRM) by transforming how organizations acquire, develop, deploy, evaluate, and retain human capital while expanding HR’s strategic role in decision-making and value creation. Despite growing scholarly attention, AI-driven HRM research remains fragmented across HR functions, theoretical perspectives, technological capabilities, and organizational contexts, limiting understanding of how AI creates value, through which mechanisms it influences employee and organizational outcomes, and under what conditions these effects emerge. This study addresses these limitations through a systematic literature review of research on AI-driven HRM published between 2011 and 1 July 2026. The review critically synthesizes the evolution, applications, enabling capabilities, value-creation mechanisms, implementation conditions, and outcomes of AI-driven HRM, with particular attention to human–AI collaboration, organizational readiness, leadership, organizational culture, AI literacy, employee trust, workforce adaptability, and responsible AI governance. It identifies key conceptual, theoretical, empirical, methodological, and contextual gaps and develops a structured agenda for future research. Building on the synthesized evidence, the study proposes an integrative framework that conceptualizes AI-driven HRM as a dynamic socio-technical capability through which AI-enabled technological resources are orchestrated with strategic HR practices, human capabilities, leadership and culture, responsible AI governance, and continuous learning to generate sustainable employee and organizational value. Contextual conditions and governance mechanisms are positioned as critical boundary conditions shaping these relationships. Lean Six Sigma DMAIC is incorporated as a complementary continuous-improvement mechanism to support the systematic measurement, analysis, improvement, and control of AI-enabled HR processes. The study advances AI-HRM scholarship by moving beyond technology-centric and function-specific perspectives toward an integrated, human-centered, strategically embedded, and responsibly governed understanding of AI-driven HRM, while providing a theoretically grounded foundation for future empirical research and sustainable organizational value creation.

items.title: Artificial Intelligence in Polypharmacy. Moving Beyond Drug Alerts Toward Patient-Specific Medication Safety
items.abstract: Polypharmacy is an increasing challenge in modern clinical practice, particularly among older adults and patients with multimorbidity, chronic kidney disease, heart failure, diabetes, frailty, or cognitive impairment. Its clinical impact extends beyond the number of prescribed medicines and reflects the interaction between therapeutic burden, comorbidities, organ dysfunction, fragmented care, changing physiological reserve, and multiple prescribers. Traditional medication review remains essential but may be limited by incomplete medication histories, time constraints, fragmented records, and the difficulty of identifying clinically meaningful drug–drug, drug–disease, and drug–patient interactions. Artificial intelligence (AI) may support safer medication management by integrating prescribing data with diagnoses, laboratory values, clinical events, and patterns of healthcare use. Potential applications include medication reconciliation, prioritization of clinically relevant interactions, renal dose adjustment, adverse drug event prediction, recognition of prescribing cascades, and identification of patients most likely to benefit from structured medication review or deprescribing. However, the value of AI in polypharmacy management should not be measured by the number of alerts generated. Its most useful role may be to help clinicians distinguish theoretical medication-related risks from those that are likely to be clinically important for an individual patient. This requires transparent recommendations, reliable data, local validation, integration into clinical workflow, and clear professional accountability. This narrative clinical viewpoint discusses the opportunities, limitations, and ethical implications of AI in polypharmacy management. It argues that AI should function as a human-centered clinical decision-support tool that improves prioritization, supports multidisciplinary medication review, and preserves clinicianled and patient-centered prescribing decisions

items.title: Artificial Intelligence in University Education: Exploring the Attitudes of Science Education Students in Makurdi, Nigeria
items.abstract: The study investigated Artificial Intelligence in University Education: Exploring the Attitudes of Science Education Students in Makurdi, Nigeria. The study employed a descriptive survey research design. The population comprised 670 (374 males and 296 females) 400-level science education students of Rev. Fr. Moses Orshio Adasu University and Joseph Sarwuan Tarka University for the 2025/2026 academic session. A sample size of 237 (102 males and 135 females) students was selected using purposive sampling technique. The instrument for data collection was "Students' Attitude toward Artificial Intelligence Integration Questionnaire (SAAIIQ)." Validated by two experts in Science Education. Cronbach's Alpha was used to determine the reliability coefficient of the instrument, and the reliability coefficient obtained was 0.85. Two research questions and one hypothesis was tested. Descriptive statistics of mean and standard deviation were used for answering the research questions, while inferential statistics of independent t-test was used for testing the hypothesis at 0.05 level of significance. The findings revealed that science education students exhibited a positive attitude toward the integration of Al in universities with a cluster mean of 3.14. The study also found no significant difference between the attitudes of male and female students toward Al integration. Students demonstrated a moderate perception toward the integration of Al in universities with a cluster mean of 2.98. The study concluded that students generally accept the use of AI in university, adequate infrastructure, institutional support, and training are necessary for its effective implementation.
